passage: On his fourth day in Delhi, Jomon had already ridden the metro end to end twice, just to watch the stations change. He ate chole kulche from a cart outside the college gate, burned his tongue and laughed. His hostel room smelled of fresh paint; he stuck a city map on the wall and circled places with a red pen. Avni, a second-year who ran the photography club, invited him on a Sunday walk through the old city, and he said yes before she finished. Amma called every night from Kottayam. 'Are you eating? Are you sleeping?' 'Amma, everything is so busy here, I'll call tomorrow,' he said, already pulling on his shoes. Only once, lying in bed with the fan clicking, did he think of the smell of rain on their veranda, and then the club's group chat buzzed and he forgot.

qa.q: Where did Avni invite Jomon to go?
qa.a: On a Sunday walk through the old city.

qa.q: What does Jomon riding the metro end to end suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He is thrilled by everything new in the city and full of restless energy 🎉

qa.q: What could help Jomon now, while the city still feels exciting?
qa.a: Keeping a short regular call with Amma even on busy days would give him a steady link to home for when the newness wears off.

qa.q: What might Amma be feeling when Jomon rushes off the phone?
qa.a: Amma may miss him and feel a little shut out, while also being glad he sounds so happy.

grounding: Shows a new student's honeymoon days in a new city, where excitement and activity push aside a brief moment of missing home.

'Look at this!' Salma held up a paper bag of pastries. 'Forty pence each at the market. Forty!'
Elizabeth, her new flatmate, laughed from the top bunk. 'You've said that about everything today.'
'Because everything is amazing. The trams! The library has a whole floor just for maps!'
'Did you call your family?'
'Tomorrow. Tonight there's the international students' quiz. You're coming.'
'I've got seminar reading...'
'Elizabeth. Quiz. Free pizza.'
'Fine.' Elizabeth climbed down. 'Your phone's buzzing, by the way.'
Salma glanced at it: Ammi, missed call, the third one. She typed, 'All good, so busy, love you ❤️,' and pocketed it. For a second her face went still. Then she grabbed her scarf. 'Come on, we'll be late. I want to see the canal at night too.'

qa.q: How much did the pastries cost at the market?
qa.a: Forty pence each.

qa.q: What might Salma's face going still for a second suggest?
qa.a: It hints at a moment of homesickness that Salma quickly pushes aside with the rush of plans.

qa.q: What small step could help Salma keep her energy and her link to home?
qa.a: She could set a short regular time to call Ammi, so home stays close while she keeps exploring.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Salma's first days?
qa.a: Elizabeth finds Salma's excitement funny and catching, and ends up coming to the quiz.

grounding: Illustrates the excitement of first days in a new city, with a missed call from home brushed aside by a rush of activity.

passage:
Vera's first week in Vienna felt like a film she'd been dropped into.

She rode the tram just to ride it. She bought a pastry every morning from a different bakery and rated them in a notebook. She signed up for the climbing club, the choir and a Tuesday language exchange, all on the same afternoon.

"You're like a tourist who lives here," said Ivan, her new flatmate, watching her unpack a fourth second-hand lamp.

"Everything's new!" Vera said. "Even the light switches."

Her mother called twice on Wednesday. Vera texted, "Can't talk, at the museum, love you!!" and felt a small twist she ignored.

That night she lay on her mattress listening to the trams and was too excited to sleep. Novi Sad felt a thousand kilometres away. It was, roughly. She didn't mind at all.

qa.q: How many clubs did Vera sign up for on the same afternoon?
qa.a: She signed up for three: the climbing club, the choir and a Tuesday language exchange.

qa.q: What was Vera feeling when she ignored the small twist after texting her mother?
qa.a: She was so excited by the new city that she pushed aside a flicker of guilt or homesickness.

qa.q: What could Vera do now to make the next stage easier?
qa.a: She could keep a regular short call with her mother, so the connection is there when the novelty fades.

qa.q: How does Ivan see Vera's first week?
qa.a: Ivan seems amused by her energy, seeing her as a tourist who lives there.

grounding: A student arrives in a new city abroad and finds everything thrilling, with homesickness pushed aside by activity.

passage:
On the first morning of trainee induction at the company campus in Hyderabad, Irawati took eleven photos of the cafeteria alone.

"There's a dosa counter AND a pasta counter," she whispered to Asif, who was also nineteen and also from a small town. "And the hostel room has a window facing a lake!"

The days ran together happily. Badminton at seven, sessions till five, biryani with the other trainees at night. She joined the dance club and the quiz team. When her father called, she talked so fast about the lake that he laughed and gave up asking whether she was eating properly.

Only once, on Thursday, did she notice she hadn't thought of home all day. She felt oddly proud, then oddly hollow, then someone knocked on the door for night badminton and she forgot it.

qa.q: How many photos of the cafeteria did Irawati take?
qa.a: She took eleven photos of the cafeteria alone.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she noticed she hadn't thought of home all day?
qa.a: She felt proud and then hollow, a brief pang of homesickness quickly covered by the rush of activity.

qa.q: What small step could help Irawati prepare for later weeks?
qa.a: She could note down what she misses when the hollow feeling comes, and share it on her calls home, so it doesn't catch her off guard later.

qa.q: How might Irawati's father feel during their calls?
qa.a: He seems happy and amused by her excitement, though he may also miss her and quietly wonder how she is really doing.

grounding: A young worker arriving at a new campus finds everything fresh and exciting, with homesickness brushed aside by activity.

passage:
Subject: I LIVE HERE NOW

Hansa!!

Okay, it's been nine days in Bengaluru and I have to tell you everything.

The weather is unreal. It rained on my first evening and I stood outside the PG in it like an idiot. My college has trees older than our whole school building. There's a stall near the gate that makes filter coffee in steel tumblers and I've had it every single day. 😊

I've joined the photography club and the debate society, and a senior invited me to a gig on Saturday. A GIG, Hansa.

Ma keeps asking if I miss home. I say of course, but honestly I haven't had time to. Maybe I'm bad for saying that.

Tell me about Guwahati. Tell me the tea shop still has the broken bench.

Gargi

qa.q: How many days had Gargi been in Bengaluru?
qa.a: Gargi had been there nine days.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when writing 'Maybe I'm bad for saying that'?
qa.a: Gargi felt excited but also a small pang of guilt, since the new city was so absorbing there was no time to miss home.

qa.q: What could Gargi do to keep home close during this busy stretch?
qa.a: Gargi could set a regular call with Ma and keep writing to Hansa, so the ties stay warm when the excitement wears off.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel reading this email?
qa.a: Hansa may feel happy for Gargi and a little left behind, missing a friend who is having adventures far away.

grounding: An email from a student in a new city shows the excitement of the first days and homesickness pushed aside by activity.
